meta.question: Can I get an allergic reaction from the COVID-19 vaccine?

question: Can I get an allergic reaction from the COVID-19 vaccine?

answers: Yes, people can have allergic reactions to any medication or biological product, including vaccines. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises that anyone with an allergy to "any component" of a vaccine should not receive that vaccine. Most allergic reactions occur shortly after vaccination, which is why the CDC recommends that individuals with a history of anaphylaxis (for any reason) be observed for 30 minutes after receiving a vaccine, while all other individuals should be observed for 15 minutes. Additionally, all vaccination sites must be equipped to provide appropriate medical treatment in the unlikely event of an allergic reaction. A previous severe allergic reaction to a vaccine—regardless of which component is suspected to have caused it—is a contraindication for receiving that vaccine in the future.

history.content: Why would the CDC initially only test those who had recently traveled to China and how long would it take to get the test results back?

The CDC initially only tested those who had recently traveled to China or who had been in close contact with someone already diagnosed with COVID-19 due to limited testing capacity.  Testing results vary widely, depending on where you get tested and what lab the test is sent to. The vast majority of test sites send the samples to a lab off-site, like Quest or LabCorp, and results generally take two to 12 days because it takes time to ship the samples, and time for the labs to process the tests.

What are the different types of tests available?
There are three types of tests to detect the COVID-19 virus: Antibody (Serology) tests, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) tests, and Antigen tests.
How do the vaccines for COVID-19 work?

The Novavax COVID-19 vaccine works by injecting the coronavirus spike protein directly into the body to prompt an immune response. In contrast, mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, such as those developed by Pfizer and Moderna, teach our bodies how to produce the spike protein to stimulate an immune response.
It’s important to note that mRNA COVID-19 vaccines do not alter your DNA; instead, they utilize the natural processes of the immune system, which is already activated by germs and viruses. We know that COVID-19 vaccines effectively help prevent severe illness and death caused by COVID-19. Scientists continue to study the effectiveness of these vaccines as new variants emerge.
The currently available COVID-19 vaccines and those still under development use one of the following methods:
- An inactivated virus
- A harmless piece of the virus
- A gene from the virus
None of these methods can cause COVID-19. When a virus is introduced to your body for the first time, your immune system launches a defense response. This includes the production of antibodies that help neutralize or eliminate the virus. If you are exposed to the same virus again, these antibodies enable your immune system to recognize and fight the virus more quickly.
Are there any contraindications to consider?
